item.title: High-efficiency solid-state electrochemical thermal switching through phonon engineering of 2D materials
item.description: arXiv:2610.35547v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reversible solid-state thermal switches with large thermal contrasts remain rare, yet are essential for advanced thermal management. Using universal machine-learned interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) and density functional theory (DFT), we screen 57 transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs), spanning the 1T and 2H phases with Li and Mg intercalation. Among the candidates, Li$_a$ZrS$_2$ combines exceptional thermal conductivity switching with low heat capacity. Lithiation to Li$_{0.125}$ZrS$_2$ reduces the cross-plane thermal conductivity from approximately 3.7 to 0.05 W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. The switching behaviour exceeds that of previously reported solid-state electrochemical thermal switches. Device-level modelling further demonstrates the potential for waste-heat recovery, with a pulsed system capturing 86\% of the energy recovered by an ideal switch. We attribute the switching behaviour to substantial softening of the Zr--Zr framework, with the mean force constant decreasing from approximately 4.2 to 1.2 eV $\mathrm{\mathring{A}}^{-2}$, alongside enhanced scattering of heat-carrying acoustic phonons. These findings establish electrochemical intercalation as a promising route to engineering thermal transport in layered materials.

item.title: Retention-constrained fine-tuning of a pre-trained aluminium MACE potential for non-equilibrium defect dynamics and plasticity
item.description: arXiv:2610.35653v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adapting a pre-trained machine-learning interatomic potential for non-equilibrium defect dynamics and plasticity requires improving defect accuracy without degrading the near-equilibrium elastic and vibrational response. Here we achieve this balance for the aluminium MACE potential QP17 by integrating conditional readout uncertainty, iterative full-parameter updates and protocol-compatible relative-energy anchoring. Sensitivities over 144 linear readout weights guide acquisition, with within-batch covariance updates and evolving neural representations. After four active-learning rounds (32 acquired configurations and 400 gradient updates), force-uncertainty acquisition reduces mean development force error from 22.43 to 21.52 meV/Angstrom, outperforming random sampling (22.70), geometry-diversity selection (22.46) and uniform training across all 104 candidate labels (22.71) under the same update budget. All three force-uncertainty runs satisfy bulk-mechanical retention criteria: historical relative-energy error decreases from 0.375 to 0.207 meV/atom, while harmonic phonon root-mean-square drift remains below 0.05 THz. Matched objective ablations reveal that relative-energy anchoring suppresses harmonic drift. Out-of-sample evaluations across planar faults, twin boundaries and grain boundaries demonstrate transferable gains in defect energies and deviatoric stresses, even though virial stresses are never fitted. A closed-loop molecular dynamics and density functional theory (MD-DFT) pilot confirms that automated acceptance gating intercepts updates that violate historical elastic-group energy or vibrational tolerances. Together, these components establish a retention-constrained fine-tuning protocol for improving plastic-deformation observables while preserving the tested bulk mechanical response.

item.title: Phonon-assisted shift-current from first-principles: application to AlN monolayer
item.description: arXiv:2610.35662v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we present a first-principles approach to investigate phonon-assisted shift current in extended systems. Our method combines the special displacement technique with real-time simulations based on the dynamical Berry phase. Merging these two frameworks enables direct access to non-linear optical responses at finite temperatures, while naturally incorporating phonon scattering and phonon-assisted electronic transitions into the time-dependent dynamics. This allows us to capture temperature-dependent features and lattice fluctuations that are essential for a realistic description of non-linear photocurrent generation. As a representative example, we apply our approach to the shift-current response of a monolayer of hexagonal AlN (h-AlN). This system provides an ideal testing ground because it features an indirect band gap and lacks inversion symmetry. Moreover, h-AlN layers of different thicknesses have been fabricated and characterized in a variety of experimental settings, opening the concrete possibility of testing our predictions. Our results demonstrate the relevance of phonon-mediated processes and the importance of temperature in determining the magnitude and spectral features of the shift current in layered materials.

item.title: Third harmonic generation in the transition metal trichalcogenides
item.description: arXiv:2610.35803v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The transition metal trichalcogenides (TMTs) are an interesting class of layered 2D materials that have strong anisotropic electrical and optical properties. We report on the polarization-dependent nonlinear optical response of exfoliated crystals at the third harmonic using non-resonant excitation with a 1560 nm femtosecond laser. All members of the TMT crystal family explored (ZrS3, HfS3, TiS3, and NbS3) display large anisotropy in their polarized third harmonic generation signal, with anisotropy ratios as large as chi_11/chi_22 ~ 6.5. From the expected nonlinear dependence of these monoclinic and triclinic crystals we extract the relative nonlinear susceptibility coefficients. We find that the anisotropy ratio is largest for ZrS3 and decreases across the family, a trend we associate with the proximity of the third harmonic energy to the strongly b-polarized absorption edge of each material. NbS3, the only triclinic crystal, displays a pronounced anisotropy in thick flakes that is strongly reduced in the thinnest flakes, which we attribute to a partial relaxation of the Peierls-type Nb-Nb dimerization that underlies the triclinic distortion. The large anisotropic nonlinear response in this crystal family sets it apart from other 2D materials and makes it particularly attractive for further investigation.

item.title: Autonomous atomistic-continuum coupling through uncertainty-aware active learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.33272v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We develop an uncertainty-aware surrogate modeling approach for coupling an atomistic kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) surface-chemistry solver with a continuum multi-species fluid dynamics solver across disparate physical length and time scales. The surrogate model predicts boundary mass fluxes for six species and their uncertainties, which the continuum solver monitors to automatically trigger additional KMC simulations when new training data are needed. This enables efficient multiscale coupling and maintains a user-specified level of accuracy. We demonstrate the approach for reactive halide-perovskite vapor deposition, which involves a multi-species vapor jet impinging on a reactive substrate. The KMC solver uses a DFT-calibrated energetics model that we construct as part of this work and provides net deposition and desorption rates for six species. With a conservative uncertainty threshold, the surrogate-coupled approach reproduces cumulative mass fluxes of the directly coupled approach with errors typically within 10-20%, while capturing the non-monotonic dependence of net deposition on species partial pressure. Importantly, the results show that detailed crystal structure need not be explicitly represented to predict quantities exchanged between atomistic and continuum solvers; species-resolved mass fluxes provide a sufficiently low-dimensional representation of the atomistic response. For this accuracy target, the autonomous online-learning approach reduces the number of required atomistic simulations by two to three orders of magnitude relative to direct multiscale coupling.

item.title: Chemical Substitution as a Route to Anomalous Surface Superconductivity in NiBi$_3$
item.description: arXiv:2610.33463v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Stabilizing two-dimensional superconductivity in a bulk superconducting material provides a unique route to exploring the interplay between superconducting condensates of different dimensionalities. Here, we present evidence for a distinct surface-associated superconducting state in Pb-substituted NiBi$_3$. NiBi$_{2.8}$Pb$_{0.2}$ exhibits a resistive onset at $T_{c,\mathrm{onset}}^{*}\approx8.1$~K, nearly twice the bulk superconducting transition temperature of approximately 4.1~K. The absence of a corresponding Meissner response or specific-heat anomaly at the higher-temperature transition supports its non-bulk origin. A cusp-like angular dependence of the critical field, well described by the two-dimensional Tinkham model, together with nonlinear current--voltage characteristics and signatures of a Berezinskii--Kosterlitz--Thouless transition, establishes the low-dimensional character of this superconducting state. Remarkably, the surface-associated superconductivity persists well beyond the bulk upper critical field, reaching a maximum ratio of $H_{c3}/H_{c2}\approx4.3$, far exceeding the conventional Saint-James--de Gennes value of 1.695. These results demonstrate that Pb substitution can stabilize an anomalously enhanced low-dimensional superconducting state in NiBi$_3$, providing a platform for investigating superconductivity at the boundary of a bulk superconductor.

item.title: Perpendicular Anisotropy and g-Factor of Sputtered Ni Films on Si(111) Studied by Angle-Dependent Ferromagnetic Resonance
item.description: arXiv:2610.33637v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Ni films with thicknesses of 312 and 1011\,\AA{} were grown on Si(111) by dc magnetron sputtering at room temperature and studied by atomic force microscopy, grazing-incidence X-ray diffraction, X-ray reflectivity, magnetometry and angle-dependent ferromagnetic resonance. Both films are polycrystalline fcc Ni with smooth surfaces, a bulk-like (111) lattice spacing and a saturation magnetization of ${\approx}480$\,emu\,cm$^{-3}$, and both are magnetized in plane. The angular dependence of the resonance field, from the film plane to the film normal, is described by a uniaxial anisotropy model with first- and second-order terms. From this model, $g = 2.160\pm0.005$ and $2.101\pm0.014$ and effective perpendicular anisotropies of $(6.0\pm0.4)\times10^{5}$ and $(4.5\pm0.6)\times10^{5}$\,erg\,cm$^{-3}$ were obtained for the thinner and thicker film, respectively. The conventional analysis of only the in-plane and perpendicular resonances gives $g$-factors that are lower by 0.02--0.04. The perpendicular linewidths give upper limits for the Gilbert damping of $\alpha \le 0.030$ and $\le 0.038$.

item.title: Aging dynamics and generalized superposition principles in carbon black-carboxymethylcellulose hydrogels
item.description: arXiv:2610.33682v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Aqueous dispersions of hydrophobic carbon black (CB) particles can be stabilized by carboxymethylcellulose (CMC), forming CB-CMC hydrogels whose microstructure is controlled by the relative CB-to-polymer content. At low CMC content, CB particles form a percolated, electrically conductive network, whereas at higher polymer content, CB particles act as isolated physical crosslinkers within an electrically insulating polymer matrix [see Legrand \textit{et al.}, Macromolecules 56, 2298-2308 (2023)]. Combining rheology and electrical impedance spectroscopy, we show that these two regimes exhibit markedly different aging dynamics. Conductive hydrogels exhibit logarithmic elastic recovery associated with a percolated CB network, whereas insulating hydrogels exhibit a combination of logarithmic and power-law stiffening, accompanied by dielectric polarization associated with confined ionic motion. The insulating hydrogels further exhibit a time-aging superposition principle, as their viscoelastic spectra measured in a time-resolved fashion can collapse onto a single master curve. Under steady shear, the viscoelastic response measured perpendicular to the flow also obeys a time--shear-rate superposition principle. Remarkably, the scaling between the shift factors under shear is reminiscent of critical-gel behavior, unlike that observed during aging at rest. Finally, time-resolved rheo-USAXS measurements performed during shear-rate cycles reveal structural rearrangements of CB particles and clusters that correlate with rheological hysteresis. These results provide a microstructural basis for understanding the nonlinear rheology of insulating CB-CMC hydrogels and establish generalized superposition principles as a unifying framework for their aging and flow behavior.

item.title: Hidden Fisher Information in Many-Body Quantum Sensors
item.description: arXiv:2610.33893v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantum Fisher information (QFI) determines the ultimate precision of a quantum sensor after optimization over all allowed measurements, but it does not quantify how difficult the optimal readout is to implement. We introduce a moment Fisher hierarchy $F_M^{(k)}$, which measures the fraction of QFI accessible to collective spin moments up to degree $k$, together with a readout-complexity scale $k_{90}$ defined by the minimum degree required to recover $90\%$ of the QFI. Applying this framework to a nonlinear collective-spin sensor, we show that many-body dynamics can preserve large QFI while transferring the optimal readout into high-rank $SU(2)$ tensor sectors inaccessible to low-order collective observables. For system sizes up to $N=100$, first moments access only $\sim 10^{-2}$ of the available QFI, while the degree required to recover $90\%$ of it grows to $k_{90}\simeq 28$. A rank-resolved analysis of the symmetric logarithmic derivative (SLD) under weak damping shows that the nonlinear protocol pushes the optimal readout toward the highest available tensor ranks while strongly depleting its low-rank weight. These results identify nonlinear tangent-space shear as the mechanism behind a finite-size readout-complexity bottleneck in many-body quantum metrology.

item.title: Momentum-selective graphene spectroscopy of moir\'e excitons
item.description: arXiv:2610.33989v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Far-field photoluminescence probes only the light-cone corner of an exciton's momentum content, whereas energy transfer to nearby graphene integrates in-plane momenta up to the inverse spacer thickness $1/z$. For a WSe$_2$/MoSe$_2$ heterobilayer we build the transition polarization $\bm{P}_n(\qv)$ of each localized moir\'e exciton from the registry-dependent vector dipole texture and use each $\bm{P}_n$ for both baths. The two baths rank the states differently: the graphene-rate ratios differ from the optical ones, their ordering inverts with spacer thickness, and the distance exponents at $z=10$\,nm spread by more than two units. These ratios are independent of the transition-dipole prefactor. Within the $C_3$-symmetric leading-harmonic model the chiral $p_+$ and $d_-$ states are also dark at normal incidence yet transfer to graphene at rates comparable to the bright ground state. Their graphene rate depends on the sign of the texture phase, a quantity invisible in far-field emission, which we determine from first principles. In a device this prediction requires a splitting, larger than the symmetry-breaking mixing, that protects the chiral partners. Graphene proximity thus acts as a momentum-selective near-field probe of moir\'e excitons, and we propose its use as a practical spectroscopy.

item.title: Designing sustainability under Earth-system rate constraints
item.description: arXiv:2610.34026v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Sustainability debates are monopolized by quantities: total energy use, material stocks, or recycling volumes. These metrics are informative, but they obscure a more fundamental constraint. On a materially closed but energetically open Earth, long-term viability is governed by rates: power density, areal power density, and the rate at which dispersed materials can be repurified under dif- fuse solar fluxes. We develop a physical framework that links technological metabolism, material dilution, and recycling limits through these rate con- straints. This perspective clarifies why many contemporary technologies remain viable only through stock drawdown and high-power buffering, and why green growth strategies often shift rather than resolve the underlying mismatch between industrial activity and Earth-system dynamics. We argue that long-term sustain- ability requires both quantitative reduction in aggregate industrial throughput toward rate-bounded regimes and the development of technologies qualitatively compatible with biospheric operating conditions.

item.title: Field misalignment effect on the in-plane magnetoresistance in the high-temperature superconductor FeSe/SrTiO3
item.description: arXiv:2610.34168v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The azimuthal angular dependence of the in-plane magnetoresistance provides a powerful probe for detecting rotational symmetry breaking in superconductors, which has significant implications for understanding the superconducting pairing symmetry and the intertwined orders. However, in two-dimensional or layered superconductors with strong anisotropy between in-plane and out-of-plane critical fields, measuring the in-plane magnetoresistance is particularly challenging as it is extremely sensitive to the field misalignment. Here we perform systematic electrical transport measurements on ultrathin FeSe films grown on SrTiO3 substrates. By remounting the same FeSe film to change the field misalignment, two qualitatively different angular dependences of the in-plane magnetoresistance are observed in the superconducting transition region, indicating the extreme sensitivity of the measurement to field misalignment. The observed anisotropic in-plane magnetoresistance can be well captured by our geometric model considering the field misalignment effect. Our work provides a practical framework for disentangling the misalignment effect and investigating the in-plane rotational symmetry breaking in two-dimensional or layered superconductors.
item.dc:creator: Jie Liu, Zihan Cui, Xiaorong Liu, Yanzhao Liu, Ziqiao Wang, Jian Wang, Yi Liu

item.title: Axion Quasibound States in the Continuum and Their Enhanced Axion Nonlinearity
item.description: arXiv:2610.34195v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Dynamical axion quasiparticles (DAQs) in condensed-matter systmes have emerged as a fascinating platform for exploring axion physics and nonlinear optical phenomena. However, the amplitude of the coherent oscillating $\theta$ field is even smaller than that of the static counterpart, making the experimental observation of DAQs particularly challenging. Here, we introduce symmetry-sensitive bound states in the continuum (BICs) physics to enable the all-optical detection of DAQs and enhance DAQ-mediated second-harmonic generation (SHG). Specifically, we uncover that DAQs induce optical shear that breaks the $C_{2z}$ symmetry of metagratings without geometric engineering, thereby converting symmetry-protected BICs into axion quasi-BICs (qBICs). In this context, the evolution of the quality factor and topological charge in momentum space, together with the appearance of optical resonances in far field associated with axion qBICs, offers achiral optical signatures for DAQ detection beyond the widely used Kerr and Faraday effects. Furthermore, by exploiting axion qBICs in the critical coupling regime to enhance fundamental optical field, we show that the SHG efficiency can be enhanced more than $10^5$-fold compared to bulk axion materials, achieving a conversion efficiency exceeding $10^{-6}~W^{-1}$. The SHG is governed by the magnetoelectric coupling, which differs from that in conventional SHG materials. Our findings establish a new approach for probing DAQs via achiral optical effects, while providing a versatile route for reconfigurable photonics and terahertz nonlinear optics.
item.dc:creator: Chang-Yin Ji, Chong Wang, Jiafang Li, Yugui Yao

item.title: MatOS: An Agent Operating System for Materials Research
item.description: arXiv:2610.34203v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Materials research relies on scattered and growing data, knowledge, and simulation tools, and a single study often spans multi-day workflows across literature analysis, computation, and experiment. Large language model agents can now retrieve materials data, operate simulation codes, and close design-synthesis-characterization loops with autonomous laboratories. However, extending these agents with new capabilities, keeping long-running tasks on track, and letting them learn from past tasks and user feedback remain difficult. Here we present MatOS, an agent operating system for materials research with three core components: (1) a layered scientific asset graph that organizes data, knowledge, tools, skills, roles, and workflows as reusable assets; (2) a stateful adaptive workflow that runs tasks as explicit execution graphs with scientific checks, so that they can be resumed and traced; and (3) evidence-driven asset evolution, which revises these assets from execution records and user feedback. On ResearchClawBench, MatOS improves on the previously best-performing agent by 11.15% with the same base model and extends the cost-score Pareto frontier. With a common base model, it outperforms Codex CLI and Claude Code, exceeding Codex CLI by 2.13% on MatTools and 4.17% on SciAgentGym. In eight research cases, MatOS narrowed more than 30 million candidate structures to 97 solid-electrolyte candidates, identified 89 halide variants with higher computed conductivity than their parent structures, linked the force errors of 11 pretrained interatomic potentials to local atomic environments, and supported two new methods that reduce errors by 3.1% and 13.6% relative to their baselines. These results show that organizing research capabilities as reusable, evolving assets enables agents to carry out long, multistage materials studies. Code is available at https://github.com/DingyangLyu/MatOS.

item.title: Controllable charge-spin conversion in sliding multiferroic metal Fe3GaTe2
item.description: arXiv:2610.34295v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Controlling charge--spin conversion within a single magnetic material is important for compact spintronic devices. Using first-principles calculations, symmetry analysis, and Wannier-based linear response, we study the Edelstein and spin Hall responses of sliding-ferroelectric bilayer \ce{Fe3GaTe2}. Two degenerate ground states with opposite interlayer sliding vectors and out-of-plane dipole moments are separated by a calculated switching barrier of about $16.3$~meV per unit cell. Magnetization orientation determines the allowed current-induced spin components, while ferroelectric switching induces component-selective sign reversals governed by $M_z\mathcal T$ for in-plane magnetization and by $M_z$ for out-of-plane magnetization. The Edelstein response is strongly energy dependent, with spin accumulation approaching $2~\hbar$ for $\mathbf m\parallel+y$ under a reference field of $1$~V/\AA. Momentum-resolved analysis links the TR-even and TR-odd Edelstein responses to $\Gamma$-centered constant-energy contours and localized interband features, respectively. Spin-conductivity contributions show the opposite momentum-space character, with broad sign-competing spin Berry curvature for TR-even and narrow Fermi-surface contours for TR-odd. The transverse spin Hall conductivity reaches $\sim10^{3}\,(\hbar/e)(\mathrm{S/cm})$ and depends strongly on ferroelectric state and magnetization direction. Magnetization rotations in the $xy$ and $xz$ planes reveal symmetry-allowed higher angular harmonics in both spin accumulation and spin-current responses. These results establish sliding-ferroelectric bilayer \ce{Fe3GaTe2} as a tunable platform for reconfigurable spin accumulation and spin-current generation.

item.title: Phase fluctuations dominated superconductivity in a thick Granular Boron-Doped Diamond film
item.description: arXiv:2610.34319v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We investigate the superconducting properties of a 1.2-{\mu}m-thick granular boron-doped diamond film, where tightly packed grains form a disordered network of Josephson junctions. The film exhibits a sharp superconducting transition at a critical temperature, T_c ~ 3 K. Its transport properties are well described by the Ambegaokar-Halperin theory of phase fluctuations. Direct measurements of the penetration depth using a two-coil mutual inductance technique reveal classic phase-fluctuation-dominated behavior: below T_c, the superfluid density (n_s) varies linearly over a wide temperature range - a hallmark of thermal phase fluctuations - before crossing over to a T^2 dependence at ultra-low temperatures. Both the large low-temperature penetration depth, {\lambda}(0) ~ 8.8 {\mu}m, and the slope of the linear ns variation in the thermal regime reveal a remarkably low superfluid stiffness in the range of 0.5-0.8 K. These results establish granular boron-doped diamond films as an excellent model system for investigating the role of long-wavelength phase fluctuations in three-dimensional superconductors.

item.title: Real-Time Correlation of Relaxation, Dephasing, and Two-level System Dynamics in Transmon Qubits
item.description: arXiv:2610.34485v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Materials improvements in transmon qubits have yielded remarkable advances in qubit lifetimes (T1)and coherence times (T2). However, state-of-the-art superconducting qubits experience temporal fluctuations in their performance, which limit gate fidelities and quantum processor performance. We observe correlated increases in qubit relaxation and dephasing rates that last for minutes to hours, which we call T1 and T2 excursions. Using interleaved lifetime and coherence time measurements, noise spectroscopy, and two-level-system (TLS) spectroscopy, we find that these excursions are caused by single or few strongly-coupled TLS defects that spectrally diffuse into resonance with the qubit frequency. Our measurement protocol provides a powerful tool for understanding the noise sources that cause temporal fluctuations in superconducting qubit performance.

item.title: Methyl radicals dynamics on (100)--(2x1):H diamond surfaces based on refined variational transition state calculations of gas-surface reaction rate coefficients
item.description: arXiv:2610.34584v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Theoretical modelling of diamond growth should ideally provide estimates of the growth rate depending on experimental conditions. To that end, a description of all possible reactions related to the competing adsorption, desorption and migration mechanisms is required. Here, we provide precise calculations of the reaction rate coefficient of methyl-related reactions on hydrogen-terminated (100) diamond surface, as $\mathrm{CH_3}$ is known to be the main growth precursor in chemical vapor deposition (CVD) growth of diamond. To achieve this goal, we successfully combined Density Functional Theory (DFT) and variational transition state theory (VTST), allowing to extend our analysis to barrierless reaction. Our rigorous treatment of the quasi-free rotation of $\mathrm{CH_3}$ adsorbates on the surface allows us to overcome numerical errors for the finite difference calculations of the vibrational spectra for evaluating the partition functions of the system. Our results suggest that the mechanism that deplete the $\mathrm{CH_3}$ concentration the most is the absorption on a surface radical site. We also evidence the anisotropy of $\mathrm{CH_3}$ migration along the dimer of the (100)-(2x1):H surface. In a more general perspective, the calculated reaction rates coefficient for methyl reactions and migration presented in this work, together with the data for hydrogen reaction and other main gas surface reactions, bridge the gap between the atomic-scale description and the large-scale modelling of diamond growth.

item.title: Spontaneous magnetic diode effect in Co$_{1/3}$TaS$_2$
item.description: arXiv:2610.34586v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: When electrons move through non-trivial spin textures in magnetic metals, conduction electrons couple to magnetic order through both their charge and their spin, acquiring non-trivial equations of motion and a dynamic spin polarization providing the foundation of spintronics. These mechanisms are, however, almost invariably reciprocal and the resistance a current encounters does not depend on its flow direction. Here we show that a chiral crystal lattice and an independently reversible chiral magnetic order together produce a diode whose forward direction is set by the magnetism rather than by the structure. In the triangular-lattice antiferromagnet Co$_{1/3}$TaS$_2$, whose chiral lattice hosts a chiral magnetic order of its own, independent handedness, we observe a pronounced nonreciprocal resistance. Unlike conventional electrical magnetochiral anisotropy, which is driven by an external magnetic field, our spontaneous magnetic diode effect arises from an internal noncoplanar spin texture with vanishing net magnetization. Symmetry analysis and model calculations show that the effect originates from the interplay of noncoplanar spin order and spin-orbit coupling, which generates a chiral, time-reversal-symmetry-breaking electronic response. Crucially, reversing the magnetic handedness reverses the sign of the nonreciprocal resistance, demonstrating magnetic control of the diode polarity.

item.title: Non-magnetic impurities as a quantum microscope of finite size effects in spin chains
item.description: arXiv:2610.34596v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Finite-size effects are ubiquitous in quantum matter, yet typically invisible in the thermodynamic limit; when system size is restricted, boundaries and confinement reveal modified spectra, correlations, and emergent phenomena. With growing access to well-controlled few-spin systems, these effects are now directly observable and offer a route to probing universal physics and enabling quantum information applications. Here, we study finite-size physics in the quasi-one-dimensional Ising-like quantum antiferromagnet Ba(Co$_{1-x}$Mg$_x$)$_2$V$_2$O$_8$ with $x = 2\%$ and $x = 5\%$, where non-magnetic Mg$^{2+}$ ions fragment the Co$^{2+}$ spin chains into finite segments. Combining inelastic neutron scattering and numerical calculations, we identify distinct regimes with fundamentally different low-energy quantum excitations: spinons confined to chain boundaries, and a cluster mode in shorter chains corresponding to a collective reversal of the N\'eel-ordered segment without classical analogue. Our results demonstrate how chemical substitution acts as a quantum microscope providing direct access to boundary-shaped excitations in strongly correlated spin systems.

item.title: Synthetic staggered fields switch Neel vectors probed by magnetic resonance
item.description: arXiv:2610.34624v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Electrical detection of antiferromagnetic order is a critical challenge for antiferromagnetic spintronics owing to their vanishing macroscopic magnetisation. While magnetic resonance has demonstrated sub-terahertz antiferromagnetic spin pumping and nonlinear magnon dynamics, its application to electrically contacted on-chip devices has room for further exploration. Here we show that magnetic resonance enables direct electrical detection of N\'eel vector states. A $180^\circ$ reversal in synthetic antiferromagnets is realised by current-driven effective fields with opposite polarisation acting on each magnetic sublayer, which we term synthetic staggered fields. The switching induces a $\pi$ phase shift of precessional motion in time, producing hysteretic rectified voltages in our phase-sensitive detection scheme. Angular-dependent resonance analysis offers further insight into the N\'eel vector directions, pointing to a model beyond the macrospin formalism. We address this by defect-incorporated micromagnetic simulations that reveal fragmented domain states after current excitation. An extracted current density of $7.4\times10^{9}$ A/m$^2$ is, to our knowledge, the lowest reported value for the room-temperature N\'eel vector switching and we show that it scales with the in-plane uniaxial anisotropy both experimentally and numerically. Synthetic staggered fields and the resonance-based methodology provide a research platform for nanoscale characterisation of electrically driven antiferromagnetic textures, guiding the development of high-frequency on-chip spintronic architectures.

item.title: Orbital-selective correlations in kagome flat bands of Co$_3$Sn$_2$S$_2$
item.description: arXiv:2610.35255v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Geometrical flat bands provide an ideal platform for studying electronic correlations and quantum-geometric effects. Although the ferromagnetic Weyl semimetal \CoSnS is generally considered a moderately correlated system, recent spectroscopy experiments have revealed a flat-band feature near the Fermi level ($\EF$) that is absent in conventional density functional theory (DFT) calculations. Using DFT plus dynamical mean-field theory and a minimal kagome model, we show that this feature arises not from heavy-fermion-like dynamical band renormalization, but from the shifting of a $d_{x^2-y^2}$ dominated geometrical kagome flat band toward $\EF$ driven by orbital- and spin-dependent self-energies. The relocated flat band enhances the local Berry curvature near $\EF$, resulting in a strongly energy-dependent anomalous Hall conductivity and a giant anomalous Nernst effect. Our findings establish an orbital-selective correlation mechanism for positioning geometrical flat bands at $\EF$, and propose anomalous thermoelectric transport as a sensitive probe of flat band induced topology.

item.title: Theoretical description of high-harmonic spectroscopy for uniaxial nematic and isotropic liquid crystals
item.description: arXiv:2610.35672v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Enabled by their controllable optical anisotropy, liquid crystals form a cornerstone of linear optical and display technologies. Bringing the versatile platform into the nonlinear regime, we explore its nonlinear optical anisotropy by high-order harmonic generation spectroscopy. Through a comprehensive study targeting gas, liquid, nematic, and crystalline phases, we present a semi-empirical tight-binding approach that provides insight into the intermolecular character of ultrafast light-driven electron dynamics across soft-matter mesophases. We demonstrate how intermolecular electron hybridization enables spectroscopic access to structural properties, such as the nematic director and order parameter. Outlining such foundational mechanisms opens avenues towards nonlinear liquid crystal devices and ultrafast soft-matter spectroscopies.

item.title: Growth Phase Map of {\alpha} and \b{eta} Tantalum as a Function of Growth Temperature and Oxygen Partial Pressure
item.description: arXiv:2610.35768v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Tantalum thin films are used in low-loss superconducting quantum circuits, yet the growth conditions governing selection of $\alpha$-Ta(110), $\alpha$-Ta(111), and metastable $\beta$-Ta on c-plane sapphire remain uncertain. We deposited 100 nm Ta films by dc magnetron sputtering on Al$_2$O$_3$(0001) at 300-900 $^\circ$C while varying the O$_2$ partial pressure from a $5.5\times10^{-11}$ Torr ultrahigh-vacuum baseline to $2.23\times10^{-4}$ Torr. Absorption-corrected X-ray diffraction texture coefficients were used to construct a ternary phase-orientation growth map in terms of temperature and the oxygen-to-Ta impingement flux ratio ($2\Phi_{O_2}/\Phi_{Ta}\leq4.8\times10^{-6}$ to 19). Without added oxygen, $\alpha$-Ta(110) dominated at every temperature. At an O$_2$ pressure of only $2.5\times10^{-9}$ Torr ($2\Phi_{O_2}/\Phi_{Ta}=2.2\times10^{-4}$), $\alpha$-Ta(111) accounted for 98-99% of the normalized texture weight from 300 to 700 $^\circ$C, decreasing to 65% at 900 $^\circ$C. Substantial $\beta$-Ta formed only at the highest oxygen dose, dominating at 300 $^\circ$C and disappearing at 900 $^\circ$C. The apparent $\beta$(001)/$\alpha$(110) selection energy of $1.07\pm0.16$ eV is comparable to the activation energy for oxygen diffusion in Ta, consistent with oxygen transport influencing phase selection. Oxygen also produced orientation-dependent changes in crystallite size and microstrain. These findings establish oxygen-controlled processing windows for phase- and orientation-selective growth of Ta films for superconducting devices.

item.title: Information-theoretic entropy imaging of quantum matter
item.description: arXiv:2610.35790v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Phase transitions can generate intricate spatial organization invisible to spatially averaged probes, yet quantitative measures of this organization remain limited. Here we develop "entropy imaging," an information-theoretic technique that harnesses lossless compression to quantify spatial complexity, predictability, and order in quantum materials. Using this approach, emergent spatial textures can be imaged and converted into an experimentally-accessible observable: the computable information density (CID), a compression-based measure of information complexity that approaches the Shannon entropy rate in the large-system limit. Applied to millikelvin microwave impedance microscopy of graphene, the method reveals a pronounced maximum in the CID near quantum Hall transitions, a quantitative measure of the information-rich spatial organization of the critical landscape. A disordered Hofstadter model reproduces this behavior and shows that the CID can identify the quantum critical point from a sequence of images, without ensemble averaging over disorder realizations. The same framework tracks fractional quantum Hall transitions and resolves isolated fractional puddles that coexist with a disordered background. By contrast, the trivial band-edge crossover in a MoSe2/WS2 moir\'e heterobilayer exhibits qualitatively different behavior, suggesting that the pronounced CID enhancement observed at the quantum Hall critical point is not simply a generic feature of a conductive-insulating crossover. We further show that the geometric information encoded in CID is not reducible to a correlation length, and it can even distinguish spatial textures with identical multifractal statistics. Together, these results establish lossless compression as a framework for quantifying emergent spatial organization in quantum materials, with portability across imaging modalities and physical systems.

item.title: Revealing the proton slingshot mechanism in solid acid electrolytes through machine learning molecular dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2503.15389v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In solid acid electrolytes CsH$_2$PO$_4$ and CsHSO$_4$, the origin of fast proton conduction has long been debated, attributed either to local proton hopping or to polyanion rotation. However, the precise role of polyanion rotation and its interplay with proton hopping remained unresolved. Nanosecond-scale molecular dynamics simulations, driven by equivariant neural network force fields, reveal a nuanced proton slingshot mechanism: protons are first carried by rotating polyanions, followed by O-H bond reorientation, and the combined motion enables long-range jumps. This mechanism challenges the conventional revolving paddlewheel model, revealing long-range transport arises from significant O-H bond reorientation assisted by only limited polyanion rotation. Despite their structural similarity, CsH$_2$PO$_4$ and CsHSO$_4$ exhibit qualitatively different transport behavior, governed by their distinct proton concentrations. In CsH$_2$PO$_4$, two rotation rates with different activation energies emerge, while CsHSO$_4$ displays a single-rate process with faster productive polyanion dynamics. The higher proton concentration in CsH$_2$PO$_4$ frustrates PO$_4$ rotation, resulting in slower dynamics than for SO$_4$ in CsHSO$_4$. In CsH$_2$PO$_4$, we further identify a unique correlation between oxygen sharing and proton transport, arising from the extra proton per polyanion. Together, our findings establish a unified framework linking polyanion rotation, proton coordination, and long-range transport, and suggest that tuning proton concentration could accelerate rotation and enhance conductivity.

item.title: Anomalous mass renormalization in two-dimensional electron systems on ultra-wide bandgap semiconductor $\beta$-Ga$_2$O$_3$
item.description: arXiv:2507.16137v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Two-dimensional electron systems (2DESs) at wide-bandgap semiconductor surfaces and interfaces are fertile ground for emergent quantum phenomena. Here, we use micro-focused angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) to resolve the momentum-space electronic structure of a surface 2DES in $\beta$-Ga$_2$O$_3$, an ultra-wide bandgap semiconductor with a band gap of 4.7 eV. In situ electron doping of cleaved, high-purity $\beta$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ single crystals produces an essentially circular Fermi surface. With the self-consistent Poisson-Schr\"odinger model, the 2D electrons are estimated to be confined within approximately 1.2 nm beneath the surface, with an internal electric field of approximately 18 MV cm$^{-1}$. Our analysis based on ARPES measurements reveals nearly a twofold increase in the electron mass at high sheet carrier densities. This trend deviates from the conventional behavior reported for wide-bandgap semiconductors and indicates mass renormalization beyond the conventional screening-based picture. Our results provide quantitative momentum-space benchmarks for the Fermi-surface geometry and density-dependent quasiparticle dispersion of the $\beta$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ 2DES, opening a route to studying density-tunable interfacial quantum states in the UWBG regime.

item.title: Electronic structure, excitonic optical response, and defect stability of RbTlCl3 from first-principles
item.description: arXiv:2508.16264v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a many-body ab initio study of the electronic structure, optical properties, excitonic effects, and defect stability of RbTlCl3. Density functional theory and many-body methods are used to investigate the properties with and without spin-orbit coupling (SOC). The indirect band gaps obtained using PBE-GGA are 0.94 and 0.95 eV with and without SOC, respectively. Optical spectra are calculated using the independent-particle approximation (IPA), IPA with scissor correction (IQPA), random-phase approximation (RPA) with local-field effects (LFEs), and the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE). The maximum imaginary dielectric function is approximately 7 at 2 eV within IQPA and decreases to 5.7 when LFEs are included. BSE calculations yield a peak value of approximately 10.8 at 1.6 eV, revealing strong excitonic effects. Four prominent bright bound excitons exhibit binding energies of 315-365 meV. The main bright exciton is localized in reciprocal space and delocalized in real space. The spectroscopic limited maximum efficiency is estimated to be 15.4% for a 0.5-micrometer-thick film. The absence of imaginary phonon frequencies and the existence of a thermodynamically stable region indicate dynamical and thermodynamic stability. Chemical-potential analysis identifies the chlorine vacancy as the most stable neutral defect under chlorine-poor conditions and the thallium vacancy under chlorine-rich conditions. These findings establish RbTlCl3 as a promising theoretical candidate for photovoltaic applications and provide insights into excitonic effects in inorganic perovskites.

item.title: Altermagnetic Signatures and Topological Textures in Ultrathin Multiferroic BiFeO$_3$
item.description: arXiv:2601.09970v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Magnetoelectric multiferroics promise low-power switching, nonvolatile memory, and signal transduction, yet practical deployment requires ultrathin films where polar and magnetic order often degrade. Uncompensated bound charge drives depolarization in ferroelectrics, while off-stoichiometry, reduced anisotropy, and charge transfer can produce magnetic dead layers. Here, we realize a multiferroic phase of BiFeO$_3$ with no dead layer, revealing signatures of emergent altermagnetism in the ultrathin limit. First-principles calculations, symmetry analysis, atomic-resolution imaging, and magnetic imaging show that short-circuit electrostatic boundary conditions and epitaxial strain drive a continuous, thickness-induced phase transition accompanied by multiferroic topological textures. At four unit cells, these boundary conditions stabilize a collinear monoclinic phase with d-wave altermagnetic order, supported by magnetic circular dichroism and spin-resolved photoemission measurements. These results establish a pathway to stabilize unconventional multiferroicity at device-relevant thicknesses, reframing scaling limits for oxide electronics.

item.title: Eutectic and peritectic equilibria in coherent binary alloys
item.description: arXiv:2602.15251v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This work extends the Cahn--Larch\'e thermodynamic framework to binary alloys in which two coherent solid phases coexist with an incoherent liquid and investigates how coherency strain energy modifies classical eutectic and peritectic equilibria. We derive equilibrium conditions for three-phase coexistence that include an elastic energy term dependent on the molar fractions of the solid phases and apply them to model binary eutectic and peritectic systems. We find that coherency stress transforms the eutectic point into a finite three-phase equilibrium field spanning a continuous range of compositions and temperatures. In systems whose equilibrium compositions are peritectically ordered, coherency stress progressively destabilizes the two-solid equilibrium without generating a stable three-phase field and can suppress the peritectic reaction entirely. This asymmetry is governed by the geometric relationship between the compositions of the phases: when the liquid composition lies between those of the two solids (eutectic configuration), the liquid serves as a thermodynamic buffer against the coherency penalty on the solid--solid pair; when it lies outside (peritectic configuration), no such mechanism is available. These results demonstrate that coherency stress can fundamentally alter three-phase equilibria involving a liquid and suggest that such effects may be significant in systems with large coherent misfits.

item.title: Nonsymmorphic Time-Reversal-Doubled Axion Insulators
item.description: arXiv:2603.01072v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The axion insulator exhibits a topological magnetoelectric effect characterized by an axion angle $\theta=\pi$, while the time-reversal-doubled axion insulator (T-DAXI) can be viewed as two copies of an axion insulator related by time-reversal symmetry. In this work, we show that a nonsymmorphic topological crystalline insulator with glide (or screw) symmetry can host the nonsymmorphic T-DAXI phase, diagnosed by the nontrivial hourglass (screw) invariant $\delta_h=1$ ($\delta_s=1$). In this phase, the partial axion angles ($\theta^\pm=\pi $) are quantized by the glide and/or screw symmetry, and the gapped surfaces realize half-quantized quantum spin Hall states. Furthermore, we show that nonsymmorphic T-DAXIs also exhibit the spin-magnetoelectric effect. Namely, an external magnetic field can induce a topological nonlocal spin polarization in real space. When the magnetic field is time-periodic, this leads to an alternating spin current detectable in experiment. Using ab initio calculations, we demonstrate that mixed bismuth monohalides Bi4Br3I and Bi4BrI3 realize the nonsymmorphic T-DAXIs. Our findings not only reveal the symmetry-enforced T-DAXIs in nonsymmorphic topological crystalline insulators, but also demonstrate the spin-magnetoelectric effect as a detectable topological spin response in nonsymmorphic T-DAXIs.

item.title: Orbitronics: orbit-spin interconversions for long range orbital propagation enabled by spin current
item.description: arXiv:2603.28075v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Orbitronics assumes long-range orbital currents, like spin currents in spintronics. However, recent theories and experiments challenge this view, showing rather local characters for orbital polarization and importance of orbit-spin conversions. In our work, angular momentum is created by ferromagnetic resonance or thermal gradients in Ni/(Pt)Ti/Au heterostructures and detected by conversion to charge current. The observed charge currents are independent of Ti thickness up to 60 nm, which is incompatible with orbital transport and Orbital Hall Effect in Ti. Instead, they depend on both Ti interfaces, evidencing spin-mediated transport in between after and before local orbit-spin interconversions.

item.title: Intrinsic i-wave altermagnetism in 2D graphene superlattices
item.description: arXiv:2604.19661v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Altermagnets feature unconventional magnetism due to their momentum-dependent spin splitting purely driven by magnetic order, for which a variety of transition-metal-based d-wave altermagnets have been proposed. However, carbon-based altermagnets in graphene structures remain elusive, even though magnetism in graphene nanostructures has been widely demonstrated. Here, we establish a symmetry-guided design principle to engineer i-wave altermagnets in graphene antidot superlattices and demonstrate the emergence of altermagnetic states in specific monolayer and bilayer graphene superlattices. By combining first principles methods and atomistic tight binding models, we show the appearance of an interaction-induced i-wave altermagnetic splitting, stemming from the intrinsic magnetic instability of 2D graphene antidot superlattices. Our work establishes a strategy to engineer i-wave altermagnetism in a graphene platform, putting forward a carbon-based platform for altermagnetic spintronics.

item.title: CrystalREPA: Transferring Physical Priors from Universal MLIPs to Crystal Generative Models
item.description: arXiv:2605.08960v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Crystal generative models mainly learn what stable crystals look like, with little explicit supervision for what makes them stable. We reveal a substantial representation gap between state-of-the-art crystal generative models and pretrained universal machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) via energy probing, and show this gap can be closed by a simple training-time alignment. We propose Crystal REPresentation Alignment (CrystalREPA), a plug-and-play framework that aligns the atom-wise hidden states of generative encoders with frozen MLIP representations through an element-aware contrastive objective, transferring stability-aware atomistic priors with marginal training overhead and no additional inference cost. Across three generative frameworks, ten MLIP teachers, and two benchmark datasets, CrystalREPA consistently improves the thermodynamic stability, structural validity, and structural fidelity of generated crystals. Equally important, we find that an MLIP's transfer effectiveness is poorly predicted by its accuracy on standard leaderboards (e.g., Matbench Discovery) but strongly predicted by the distinguishability of its atom-wise representation space, yielding a practical, accuracy-independent criterion for selecting MLIP teachers for generative transfer. Code is available at https://github.com/Chengqian-Zhang/CrystalREPA.

item.title: Charge dynamics at nitrogen impurities and nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond
item.description: arXiv:2605.24768v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center in diamond is the prototype quantum defect that enables a variety of diamond-based quantum technologies. However, charge-state instability and spectral diffusion, often induced by substitutional nitrogen impurities (N$_{\rm C}$), remain key challenges for device performance. Here, we employ first-principles density functional theory calculations to quantitatively investigate nonradiative carrier capture processes mediated by multiphonon emission at both the NV center and the N$_{\rm C}$ impurity. For relevant cases, we also compute the rates of radiative and thermal emission processes. For N$_{\rm C}^0$ $\to$ N$_{\rm C}^-$, we obtain an electron capture coefficient of $2.2 \times 10^{-8}$ cm$^3$s$^{-1}$ at 300 K. Both the magnitude and temperature dependence are in excellent agreement with experimentally measured capture cross sections. Electron capture at N$_{\rm C}^+$ is even faster, with a capture coefficient of $1.0 \times 10^{-4}$ cm$^3$s$^{-1}$ at 300 K. For the NV center, we find that carrier capture rates involving only the ground states of NV$^0$ and NV$^-$ are negligibly slow. However, capture into the excited states (NV$^{0*}$ and NV$^{-*}$) is significantly faster. In particular, the capture coefficient for the hole capture process NV$^-$ $\to$ NV$^{0*}$ is as large as $1.8 \times 10^{-7}$ cm$^3$s$^{-1}$ and largely temperature-independent. Hole capture at NV$^-$ will thus occur via nonradiative capture into an excited state of NV$^{0}$ followed by fast radiative decay to the NV$^0$ ground state. Similarly, electron capture at NV$^0$ will occur via the NV$^0$ $\to$ NV$^{-*}$ $\to$ NV$^-$ pathway, but with a lower nonradiative capture coefficient ($2.1 \times 10^{-9}$ cm$^3$s$^{-1}$ at 300 K). Our calculated capture coefficients and rates provide essential information for analyzing charge-state dynamics.

item.title: Why Fe doping kills photoluminescence in CsPbCl$_3$ but not in CsPbBr$_3$: Role of midgap Fe 3$d$ states and electron-phonon coupling
item.description: arXiv:2606.04714v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Understanding the impact of transition-metal doping on the optoelectronic properties of halide perovskite nanocrystals is essential for their rational design in photonic applications. We establish the microscopic origin of photoluminescence (PL) quenching in Fe-doped CsPbCl$_3$ using spin-polarized density functional theory calculations. The emergence of Fe 3$d$ midgap states creates efficient electron-trapping centres that drive nonradiative recombination, accounting for the reduced PL intensity. Extending this analysis to Fe-doped CsPbX$_3$ (X = Cl, Br), we show experimentally that although PL intensity is suppressed in both systems relative to their pristine counterparts, their high-doping behaviour diverges: CsPbCl$_3$ becomes completely non-emissive, whereas CsPbBr$_3$ retains a finite, saturated PL intensity. Despite this contrast, electronic structure calculations reveal nearly identical midgap states in both materials, indicating that electronic effects alone cannot explain the distinct PL responses. Phonon calculations likewise fail to capture this difference. In contrast, electron-phonon coupling calculations based on the deformation potential approach reveal significantly stronger coupling in Fe-doped CsPbCl$_3$, enabling efficient dissipation of electronic excitation energy into lattice vibrations and leading to complete PL quenching. These results identify electron-phonon coupling as the key factor governing halide-dependent PL quenching and provide a unified microscopic framework for dopant-induced nonradiative processes in halide perovskites.

item.title: Implications of an analysis of the shear transformation of a zone of an oblate spheroid for dislocation theory, grain boundary sliding and superplasticity
item.description: arXiv:2606.29061v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Grain boundary sliding models of superplastic flow take the elementary event to be the shear of an oblate-spheroidal unit embedded in a solid matrix, whose rate follows transition state theory. The mechanics of this unit, and the assumptions linking it to dislocations and macroscopic flow, have not been stated explicitly. Here the unit is analysed as an Eshelby inclusion, a continuum, mathematical treatment without using physical concepts. The analysis gives closed-form shear and volumetric energy coefficients ($0.4456$ and $0.8889$ for aspect ratio $1/2$ and Poisson ratio $1/3$) and shows that the shear stress of the unit is a force dipole, decaying as $r^{-3}$ and changing sign with direction, unlike a dislocation. The inputs, assumptions and proposals needed to connect this unit of shear to dislocation theory and superplastic flow are then stated and classed as experimentally validated, physically realistic or fitting constants. Under three such proposals, a row of about four units acquires the Peierls-Nabarro profile of a full dislocation, and two to three units that of a Shockley partial; the Peierls and Frank-Read stresses and the stacking-fault energy then follow from experimental inputs. With the unit energy as the free energy of activation and strains fitted to superplastic data, the flow law reproduces all 52 measured strain rates of a Cu alloy within an order of magnitude. Molecular-dynamics calculations for Cu outline the extension to dislocation emission, mesoscopic grain boundary sliding and the inverse Hall-Petch effect. This gives phenomenological models of superplastic flow a mechanical basis.

item.title: Raman Signatures of Lithium Ion Dynamics in LLZO Garnet Electrolytes: Atomistic Insights from MD-Raman Calculations
item.description: arXiv:2608.04690v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Lithium lanthanum zirconate (LLZO) garnets are among the most promising solid electrolytes for next-generation batteries owing to their high ionic conductivity, chemical stability, and compatibility with lithium metal. Raman spectroscopy is commonly employed to distinguish the highly conductive cubic phase from the poorly conductive tetragonal phase of LLZO, yet the atomistic origin of these spectral differences and their direct connection to Li-ion transport remain unresolved. Here, we close this gap by comparing computed and experimental Raman spectra for the tetragonal, cubic, and Ta-doped variants of LLZO, with the computed spectra obtained from the MD-Raman approach that combines machine-learning molecular dynamics with first-principles polarizability calculations. We show that the contrasting ionic transport behavior across these LLZO variants is encoded in the vibrational dynamics of the lithium sublattice and gives rise to distinct features in their Raman spectra. A symmetry-resolved analysis further reveals that experimentally observed Raman peaks do not correspond to individual normal modes, but instead arise from overlapping contributions of multiple symmetry channels, challenging conventional peak-assignment approaches. By explicitly connecting experimentally accessible Raman signatures to the underlying atomic-scale dynamics, our results show how Raman spectroscopy can move beyond empirical phase identification toward a microscopic probe of Li-ion dynamics in lithium garnet electrolytes.

item.title: The crossmetric tensor and the geometrical meaning of the imaginary numbers
item.description: arXiv:2608.05113v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The product of two Cartesian quaternions can be written as a quadratic form based on a 4x4 matrix made of the imaginary numbers i,j,k introduced by Hamilton. We generalized this matrix to non-Cartesian bases, and showed that the matrix is made of the metric and the cross tensors. We called it crossmetric tensor. Its symbols are ia,ib,ic; they are the elementary crystallographic quaternions. We determined the crossmetric tensors for the six crystal families. We also showed that any unit crystallographic quaternion can be geometrically represented by an infinity of pairs of oriented planes intersecting along the vectorial component of the quaternion such that the angle between them is the semiangle of the rotation. The composition of quaternions follows the intuitive source-target rule. The elementary quaternions ia,ib,ic are geometrically represented by pair of perpendicular and oriented planes intersecting along the axis a,b,c, respectively. Three other complementary quaternions were also introduced. They are the pairs of planes ma, mb, mc. The elementary quaternions follow Hamilton rules on the squares of imaginary numbers. The complementary quaternions follow Hamilton rules on the bi and tri-products. For Cartesian basis, the quaternions i,j,k appear as a specific case of crystallographic quaternions. They are formed by the pairs of perpendicular faces of the cube mx, my, mz.

item.title: Dimensional Control of Excitonic Interactions in Exfoliated 2D Molecular Crystals
item.description: arXiv:2609.09923v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Excited states in molecular crystals depend on intermolecular coupling, charge-transfer interactions, dielectric screening and molecular packing. How reduced dimensionality modifies these interactions when molecular packing structure is preserved remains unclear. Here we demonstrate that tetracene and three other molecular crystals can be mechanically exfoliated into mono-, few- or multilayer flakes, exploiting the top-down approach established for inorganic layered materials. Electron diffraction confirms that exfoliated tetracene retains long-range crystalline order and nearly bulk-like in-plane lattice parameters. This structural fidelity enables systematic thickness-dependent spectroscopy with limited changes in molecular packing. With decreasing thickness, the Davydov splitting diminishes, whereas the Stokes shift increases to nearly three times its bulk-like value, indicating enhanced excited-state relaxation. The photoluminescence 0-0/0-1 intensity ratio also rises, suggesting greater exciton delocalization. Compared with exfoliated tetracene, assembly-grown crystals exhibit lattice contraction and larger Davydov splitting. Analysis within the Frenkel-charge-transfer mixing framework qualitatively accounts for the Davydov-state energy shifts and splitting in terms of molecular packing, intermolecular coupling and dielectric screening. Our results show that intermolecular interactions, excited-state relaxation and exciton coherence can be systematically tuned by varying layer number, demonstrating the feasibility and utility of extending dimensional control of inorganic 2D materials to molecular crystals.

item.title: Towards a Metal-Organic Framework with Pore-Confined Electrons
item.description: arXiv:2609.13939v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Electrides are an unconventional class of materials in which electrons are localized in crystallographic void spaces rather than solely around atomic nuclei, giving rise to appealing properties such as low work functions, strong electron-donating character, and even superconductivity. Here, we use ab initio methods to investigate metal-organic framework (MOF) electrides, a new class of materials that combines the interstitial electrons of electrides with the permanent porosity and chemical tunability of MOFs. These materials host pore-confined electrons: occupied electronic states localized in the pore space and with bands slightly below or crossing through the Fermi level. Using density functional theory calculations, we establish several design rules for stabilizing pore-confined electrons in MOFs via an anion-electron exchange process and identify candidate MOF electrides. As a proof-of-concept, we also demonstrate that the pore-confined electrons can directly facilitate chemical reactions, substantially lowering the activation barrier for H2 dissociation without requiring adsorption at a surface site. We envision that pore-confined electrons in nanoporous materials may enable a fundamentally new type of catalysis in which chemical reactions take place in the pore space, driven by electron-centered active sites.

item.title: Disentangling spin polarization from driven circular ionic motion in EuTiO$_3$
item.description: arXiv:2609.28214v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Coherently driven circular ionic motion has been reported to produce large helicity-dependent optical responses attributed to transient magnetization. However, the microscopic nature and magnitude of this phenomenon, sometimes referred to as dynamical multiferroicity, remain strongly debated. Here, we directly study the connection between ionic circulation induced by a high-field circular terahertz (THz) drive and its effect on the spin system of EuTiO$_3$ using X-rays. This material exhibits an optical response consistent with the putative magnetic signal observed in related non-magnetic materials. Furthermore, the presence of Eu$^{2+}$ ions enables the use of X-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD) to test for the creation of transient spin polarization. Simultaneously, ultrafast X-ray diffraction (XRD) measures the circular ionic motion from which we determine the mechanical angular momentum. We find a classical ionic contribution of $3\times10^{-8}~\mu_B$ from XRD and upper limits of $0.03~\mu_B$ and $0.11~\mu_B$ from the sensitivity of XMCD at the europium $M_5$ and $L_2$ edges, probing the $4f$ and $5d$ shells of Eu$^{2+}$, respectively. These observations show that large-amplitude circular ionic motion in this system is not accompanied by a detectable spin polarization despite the clear signature in the optical data, with the XMCD upper bounds and classical contribution differing by many orders of magnitude.

item.title: Toward catalyst-mediated growth of diamond and cubic boron nitride wires
item.description: arXiv:2609.33478v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sustained catalyst-mediated growth of diamond and cubic boron nitride (cBN) wires has yet to be established reproducibly, although related methods produce carbon and BN nanotubes and many elemental and compound nanowires. I hypothesize that a retained contact between a catalyst and an existing tetrahedral crystal can sustain wire extension under conditions that do not nucleate that crystal on an otherwise comparable unseeded catalyst. The prediction is repeated, vapor-derived target-phase extension during an interval in which matched unseeded contacts do not nucleate that phase. I develop tests using diamond seeds, SiC starter wires and cBN seeds, separating the conditions used to establish the contact from those used for continuation. Worked estimates distinguish bulk precipitation driving forces from sidewall costs and show why increased carbon activity alone cannot select diamond over graphite. Comparisons with established synthesis identify the roles of pressure, hydrogen and activated nitrogen that must be retained or replaced. Isotope tracing, local structural measurements and time-dependent growth distinguish continued incorporation from seed consumption, conversion and etching. Nanometer, micrometer and larger wires could provide electrically insulating thermal connections, mechanical probes and reinforcing filaments.

item.title: Coherent Phonon Generation from Prethermal Carrier Populations in a Semiconductor
item.description: arXiv:2610.18279v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ultrafast laser excitation of carriers in semiconductors often results in the creation of fully symmetric coherent optical phonons, typically understood in terms of a thermalized transient carrier population. We test this understanding with systematic measurements and first-principles calculations of the photon-energy dependence of ultrafast-laser-driven coherent phonon generation in tellurium, using excitation wavelengths around the electronic band gap. We observe that, contrary to the expectations of models assuming a thermalized carrier population, the coherent amplitude of the fully symmetric $A_1$ mode changes only weakly when tuning wavelength across the band gap. The measured spectral dependence is instead reproduced by a transition-resolved prethermal force weighted by optical matrix elements and band- and momentum-dependent $A_1$ deformation potentials. Fitting this model to the data yields an excited transition state lifetime of a few femtoseconds. These results identify transition selectivity, rather than a thermalized total carrier density, as a key factor controlling coherent-phonon generation in semiconductors excited near a band gap.

item.title: Symmetry-selected extreme shear compliance in a stable carbon monolayer
item.description: arXiv:2610.19168v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Extreme stiffness contrasts between loading modes usually require architected metamaterials with compliant hinges, whereas covalent crystals rarely exhibit such behavior intrinsically. Here, density functional theory calculations of the complete in-plane elastic tensors of four tetragonal carbon monolayers reveal a more than 50-fold spread in shear stiffness, despite less than a twofold variation in axial stiffness and the same symmetry-allowed tensor form. Twin T-graphene shows the strongest contrast: its shear constant, $C_{66}=3.03$~N m$^{-1}$, is 47 times smaller than in graphene and yields a shear Kelvin eigenvalue 29 times below the two normal-strain eigenvalues, while the Born stability criteria hold. This shear constant revises an earlier inference of elastic isotropy based on normal strains alone. Constrained relaxations and symmetry-resolved mode analysis identify the mechanism as a $B_{2g}$ counter-torsion of the carbon sublayers about the mid-plane bonds, which removes 96.3% of the clamped-ion shear stiffness with bond-length changes below 0.15%. An internal-coordinate model quantifies this cancellation, identifying internal relaxation, rather than weak bonding, as the origin of the soft channel. The resulting anisotropy predicts transverse sound velocities of 1.95 km s$^{-1}$ along [100] and 10.62 km s$^{-1}$ along [110], a testable acoustic signature. Phonon calculations, ab initio molecular dynamics at 300 K, and large-deformation simulations indicate that the soft channel is dynamically stable, preserves the local bonding, and persists beyond the harmonic regime. Our results show how bonding topology enables extreme mode-selective elasticity through internal relaxation in a mechanically stable covalent crystal.

item.title: Reticulating Local Dynamics in Three-Dimensional Covalent Organic Frameworks
item.description: arXiv:2610.24418v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In covalent organic frameworks (COFs), the geometry of the building units predetermines the structure of the framework, yet comparable design principles relating the COF linkers to the local motions that govern guest adsorption and diffusion as well as mechanical response have remained beyond reach. Here, we combine synchrotron X-ray pair distribution function (PDF) analysis with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations accelerated by machine learning interatomic potentials to resolve and compare the local dynamics of two three-dimensional imine-linked COFs, chosen to differ in the geometry and rigidity of one of their two building units. Both are constructed from the same 4-connected square planar linker, $4,4',4'',4'''$-(pyrene-1,3,6,8-tetrayl)tetraaniline (PyTTA), reticulated with the 12-connected nanographene hexakis{[3,5-bis($p$-formylphenyl)-4,6-dimethoxyphenyl]}hexabenzocoronene to give COF-412, {[(HBC-LA$_{12}$)(PyTTA)$_3$]}$_{\mathit{imine}}$, and with the 6-connected triptycene 2,3,6,7,14,15-hexakis(4-formylphenyl)triptycene to give COF-564, {[(Trip-CHO)$_2$(PyTTA)$_3$]}$_{\mathit{imine}}$. The PDF-MD approach resolves the amplitude, the time scale, and the spatial extent of the motion of all COF linkers, separating the limited libration of the fused aromatic cores from the larger reorientational tilts of the pendant aryl rings they carry and from the translation of whole linkers within the net. The simulations further reveal that exchanging the nanographene- for the triptycene-based linker tunes the equilibrium tilt and the positional probability density of PyTTA, raising the tilt amplitude of its linker partner, and, notably, strengthens the coupling between the translations of neighbouring linkers. This approach provides a blueprint for understanding local dynamical properties in COFs, and shows them to be selectable through the choice of building unit and amenable to design.

item.title: Decoding Composition-Structure-Performance Relations in Sodium Layered Oxide Positive Electrode Materials
item.description: arXiv:2610.30591v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Layered sodium transition-metal (TM) oxides, Na$_x$TMO$_2$, are among the most promising sodium-ion positive electrode materials, yet their Na/vacancy orderings, layer stacking sequences, and cooperative Jahn--Teller distortions are known only for a few single-TM compounds. We compile the Na/vacancy orderings reported in earlier studies into a single library of 41 unique orderings and apply this uniformly to five single-TM and all ten Na$_x$TM$_{0.5}$TM$'_{0.5}$O$_2$ oxides (TM = Ti, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni), screening more than 120,000 structures with machine-learning interatomic potentials prior to 1,025 accurate first-principles calculations. The phase diagrams explain the observed O3/P3/O1 sequences and voltages, and the O3-to-P3 competition hinges on ordering energies of a few meV per atom that scalar descriptors, such as the cationic potential and the interlayer-slab distance, miss. Our extensive analysis reveals that the redox couples form a nearly partner-independent ladder, Ti$^{3+/4+}$ $<$ Mn$^{3+/4+}$ $<$ Co$^{3+/4+}$ $<$ Ni$^{2+/3+}$ $<$ Fe$^{3+/4+}$, explaining pristine charge transfer and the oxidation sequence. Van Vleck analysis of every TMO$_6$ octahedron reveals that TM mixing suppresses the cooperative Jahn--Teller distortions of Mn$^{3+}$ and Ni$^{3+}$ through charge transfer to Jahn--Teller-inactive states or dilution of Jahn--Teller-active centers. We formulate an energy-density-versus-strain map that yields a design rule: a high-voltage couple without Jahn--Teller strain, which Mn$^{4+}$/Ni$^{2+}$ charge transfer realizes in Na$_x$Mn$_{0.5}$Ni$_{0.5}$O$_2$, the most practical composition. We release the ordering-resolved dataset as a training set for subsequent training of accurate machine-learning interatomic potentials.

item.title: Poly(vinylidene fluoride) under finite electric displacement fields: a removable $\alpha\!\to\!\delta$ reorientation barrier and a persistent first-order $\delta\!\to\!\beta$ conformational change
item.description: arXiv:2610.31926v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The $\alpha$, $\delta$, and $\beta$ phases of PVDF are interconverted by electrical poling and mechanical drawing, yet the thermodynamics under a controlled electrical boundary condition has not been established from first principles. We evaluate the zero-temperature free energy at fixed electric displacement $D$ from van der Waals density-functional calculations along two constrained coordinates in a common 24-atom cell: a tilt of the gauche C--C bonds that maps antipolar $\alpha$ onto polar $\delta$ (cell change $<1\%$), and a backbone torsion that straightens TG$^+$TG$^-$ chains into all-trans $\beta$ (chain-repeat strain $10.6\%$). As $D$ increases from 0 to $0.30$~C\,m$^{-2}$, the lowest homogeneous free energy switches from $\alpha$ to $\delta$ at $D_{c1}=0.046$~C\,m$^{-2}$ and from $\delta$ to $\beta$ at $D_{c2}=0.157$~C\,m$^{-2}$. At $T=0$ with domain-wall energy neglected, a $\delta$ multidomain state lies $14.3$~meV per cell below homogeneous $\alpha$ at every $D$. A $\Gamma$-point harmonic estimate suggests that vibrations reverse this ordering at room temperature. $\delta$ and $\beta$ coexist for $0.11<D<0.21$~C\,m$^{-2}$ at $E^*=0.69$~GV\,m$^{-1}$, independent of the screening constant. The tilt barrier falls from $0.66$~eV per cell at $D=0$ to $17$~meV at $D=0.30$~C\,m$^{-2}$ (below $k_BT$ at $300$~K), while the torsion barrier remains $0.66$~eV at $D_{c2}$ and $0.34$~eV at $D=0.30$~C\,m$^{-2}$, so $\delta\to\beta$ stays first order. Much of the difference traces to the path effective charge ($0.28e$ for the tilt, $0.18e$ for the torsion). Scaling shows the tilt barrier would survive with the torsion charge; the smaller torsion charge accounts for about half the barrier it retains. The landscape accounts for why a field produces $\delta$ and why $\beta$ is reached by drawing, and suggests that raising that charge could let a field alone produce $\beta$.

item.title: Robust spin splitting and fermiology in the layered altermagnet CoNb4Se8
item.description: arXiv:2502.20010v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Altermagnetism defies conventional classifications of collinear magnetic phases, combining compensated magnetization with momentum-dependent, nonrelativistic spin splitting. While altermagnetic band splitting has been established in three-dimensional compounds such as MnTe and CrSb, layered altermagnets remain far less explored spectroscopically. Here, combining termination-resolved micro-ARPES, fine photon-energy mapping, spin-ARPES and density functional theory, we map the three-dimensional fermiology of the layered g-wave altermagnet CoNb$_4$Se$_8$, obtained by ordered Co intercalation of 2H-NbSe$_2$. We resolve the spin-split branches of the altermagnetic pairs directly in the raw photoemission spectra and, with spin-ARPES at these experimentally identified momenta, show the reversal of the spin polarization at opposite momenta and between two regions of the sample, consistent with opposite time-reversal domains, and its absence along the symmetry-protected nodal $\Gamma$--K direction. We further report a weak low-temperature anomaly near $T_0\approx50$ to 60 K, detected by magnetometry, temperature-dependent micro-ARPES and ultrafast reflectivity, whose microscopic origin remains open. These results provide a momentum-resolved benchmark of the electronic structure of a layered altermagnet.

item.title: Unconventional Materials for Light Dark Matter Detection
item.description: arXiv:2507.07164v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose the use of several unconventional materials as detectors for dark matter with mass beneath the MeV scale. These include the transition-metal dichalcogenide TiSe$_2$ hosting a low-energy plasmon in the charge-density-wave phase, Sr$_2$RuO$_4$ containing a low-energy acoustic demon mode, and hole-doped diamond with tunable optical and acoustic plasmon frequencies. We perform first-principles density functional theory computations of their loss functions at non-vanishing momenta and establish their reach into light dark matter parameter space. We show that due to intense low-energy plasmon modes -- of different microscopic origin in each -- the reach of detectors based on these materials could surpass existing proposals by several orders of magnitude for both dark matter scattering and absorption on electrons. The anisotropic response of these materials, which enables directional detection, renders them exceptionally strong detector candidates, motivating the design and fabrication of future devices.
