item.title: Subspace-Protected Topological Phases and Bulk-Boundary Correspondence
item.description: arXiv:2508.20908v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: While tremendous research has revealed that symmetry enriches topological phases of matter, more general principles that protect topological phases have yet to be explored. In this Letter, we elucidate the roles of subspaces in free-fermionic topological phases. A subspace property for Hamiltonians enables us to define new topological invariants. It results in peculiar topological boundary phenomena, i.e., the emergence of an unpaired zero mode or zero-winding skin modes, characterizing subspace-protected topological phases. We establish and demonstrate the bulk-boundary correspondence in subspace-protected topological phases. We further discuss the interplay of the subspace property and internal symmetries. Toward application, we also propose possible platforms possessing the subspace property.

item.title: SymADiT: Symmetry-Aware Crystal Generation with Latent Flow Matching
item.description: arXiv:2605.10115v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Tackling the task of crystal generation, we aim to enhance the previously proposed, symmetry-agnostic, All-atom Diffusion Transformer (ADiT) by introducing SymADiT, a symmetry-aware variant. To do so, we use a representation of crystals based on Wyckoff positions. We follow ADiT and perform generative modelling in latent space, adapted to our symmetry-aware representation. By forcing the output of the generative model to adhere to the symmetry restrictions imposed by the generated crystal's space group and each atom's Wyckoff position, the generated crystals exhibit more realistic symmetry properties. We benchmark our method against both symmetry-aware and symmetry-agnostic models for crystal generation and show competitive performance, generating stable, symmetric, and physically plausible crystals with only an off-the-shelf Transformer architecture. Our code is available at https://github.com/Karmush21/SymADiT.

item.title: Evaluating the Structural Basis for Polar Altermagnet Candidate Ca$_{3}$(Ru,Ti)$_{2}$O$_{7}$
item.description: arXiv:2606.16181v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The interplay between polar and altermagnetic orders remains largely unexplored in the broader landscape of correlated electron systems. Density functional theory (DFT) within the PBEsol + $U$ treatment propose Ca$_{3}$Ru$_{2}$O$_{7}$ as a polar altermagnet, reliant on the transformation of the experimentally reported $Bb2_{1}m$ phase to a lower symmetry $Pn2_{1}a$ structure. Here, we perform a targeted search for the $Pn2_{1}a$ phase using synchrotron X-ray diffraction on single crystals of Ca$_{3}$Ru$_{2}$O$_{7}$ and Ca$_{3}$(Ru$_{0.99}$Ti$_{0.01}$)$_{2}$O$_{7}$. No diffraction signature of the $Pn2_{1}a$ structure is detected down to 20 K within experimental limits. Through diffraction simulations, we translate this result into a quantitative upper bound on the symmetry breaking distortion amplitude, which we find to be significantly smaller than the DFT predicted distortion. Our DFT calculations further motivate dilute Ti substitution ($\lesssim 2\%$) as an alternative route to stabilize the low symmetry phase, for which we again find no clear evidence for this putative $Pn2_{1}a$ structure that hosts altermagnetism. Our findings indicate that PBEsol + $U$ over-stabilizes a $Pn2_{1}a$ distortion, and the measured bounds provide benchmark for future calculations. Ti substitution exceeding $\sim$3% reveals a chemically tunable polar altermagnetic phase within the $Bb2_{1}m$ structure and we theoretically demonstrate that the spin-splitting can be tuned by Ti substitution. By combining DFT, diffraction simulations and synchrotron X-ray measurements, our study demonstrates a general methodology to quantify subtle structural distortions that underlie emergent electronic and magnetic phases.

item.title: Ab initio calculations of $^{229}$Th band-to-band internal conversion rate in $^{229}$ThO$_2$
item.description: arXiv:2607.08941v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present an ab initio calculation of the band-to-band internal-conversion rate of the $\hbar\omega_{\rm nuc} \approx 8.35$ eV isomeric transition in $^{229}$ThO$_2$. Because the nuclear transition energy exceeds the electronic band gap of ThO$_2$, the isomer can decay nonradiatively by resonantly promoting a valence electron into the conduction band. We formulate this process as a Brillouin-zone sum over vertical interband transitions weighted by local Th-centered hyperfine matrix elements, which are evaluated directly from all-electron full-potential linearized augmented-plane-wave Bloch spinors. A finite nuclear magnetization model is included to regularize the short-range hyperfine interaction and to account for the Bohr-Weisskopf effect. After applying scissor shifts to span the experimentally reported ThO$_2$ band gaps, we find calculated internal-conversion lifetimes in the range of $1-16~\mu{\rm s}$. The lifetime increases strongly as the band gap approaches $\omega_{\rm nuc}$ because the resonant interband phase space at the nuclear transition energy is reduced. For the larger reported ThO$_2$ gaps, the calculated lifetime is comparable to the measured conversion-electron M\"ossbauer lifetime [Nature 648, 300 (2025)]. Our analysis implies that choosing solid-state hosts with band-gap values slightly lower than $\omega_{\rm nuc}$ can optimize solid-state nuclear clock performance with internal-conversion electron readout.

item.title: Full-data accuracy with fewer labels for training and fine-tuning machine-learning force fields
item.description: arXiv:2607.14486v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Machine-learning force fields (MLFFs) are reliable only near their training distribution, making efficient construction of diverse training sets a major bottleneck for both train-from-scratch and foundation fine-tuning workflows. Active learning can reduce this cost, but standard model-committee uncertainty is impractical for foundation MLFFs because each committee member requires a separate fine-tuning run. We present an active-learning workflow based on last-layer-projection regression (LLPR), a forward-pass-cheap per-configuration uncertainty estimator. Across molecular, condensed-phase, and electrolyte systems, LLPR identifies compact, high-value training sets that recover full-data accuracy using only a small fraction of electronic-structure labels. In foundation-model fine-tuning, LLPR-selected configurations approach the practical fine-tuning ceiling with substantially fewer labels than random selection. In iterative electrolyte fine-tuning, LLPR detects unphysical local coordination before new labelling, calibrates uncertainty in force-error units, and supports retrospective convergence monitoring. The resulting models reproduce reference density and Li--O coordination structure, providing a scalable uncertainty-quantification strategy across MLFF training regimes.

item.title: First-Principles Wannier Representation of Proximity Effects
item.description: arXiv:2607.25690v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Proximity effects in layered heterostructures are commonly represented by static parameters fitted to first-principles band structures, an approximation that usually discards the energy dependence of interlayer hybridization, momentum transfer, and spatial structure. We address this limitation by deriving a dynamical proximity operator directly from density functional theory by downfolding the heterostructure Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian onto a fixed low-energy target Wannier subspace. We demonstrate the method for three different graphene heterostructures coupled to magnetic and semiconducting substrates. Graphene/hBN/Co(0001) exhibits proximity-induced exchange resonances driven by hybridization with Co states. Graphene/PtSe$_2$ develops a sublattice-selective, intervalley-coherent, proximity-induced coupling. For graphene/WSe$_2$, we identify the spatial modulation of both Rashba and valley-Zeeman proximity-induced spin-orbit couplings. The method determines the full microscopic structure of the proximity coupling from first principles, providing input for transport and correlated-phase calculations.

item.title: Multiphysics simulation of all-optical switching and sequential magneto-optic readout in an integrated Si$_3$N$_4$/GdFeCo waveguide
item.description: arXiv:2608.22969v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In an integrated all-optical magnetic device, a guided pulse writes a magnetic state and a later optical signal reads it out. We study both steps for an 8 nm GdFeCo film inserted across a Si$_3$N$_4$ waveguide. A three-dimensional dispersive finite-difference time-domain calculation gives the energy absorbed from an 800 nm pump pulse. This energy drives a four-temperature model and calibrated stochastic two-sublattice Landau-Lifshitz-Bloch dynamics. After relaxation, a separate 532 nm probe is propagated through the fixed magnetic state for the optical readout. At the reference pump fluence, the model reverses 0.859 of the film from either saturated state. The switched fraction remains within 0.81-0.87 over a 2.4-fold range of incident fluence. A threshold rule applied to the local absorption map reproduces the five three-dimensional simulation points to within $8\times10^{-4}$, showing that, within the model, incomplete reversal results from non-uniform guided-mode absorption. When the film starts from zero magnetization, thermal noise orients the recovered local moments at random; over 16 realizations, $0.502 \pm 0.004$ of the cells end with a negative $x$ component of the FeCo moment. Among the simulated states, the probe transmission, reflection, and absorption fractions vary by at most 0.02. The magnetic Faraday and Kerr rotations are much more sensitive and become about 12 and 130 times smaller, respectively, in the stochastically recovered state than in a saturated film. The reflected signal also contains a magnetization-independent geometric background, which can be removed by subtracting a reference signal. These results link the switching efficiency to the guided-mode absorption profile and predict polarization-based readout of the simulated magnetic states. The model assumes a homogeneous film and neglects spatial exchange stiffness and subsequent domain coarsening.

item.title: Splicing an exact local self-energy into $GW$: tests on small Hubbard clusters
item.description: arXiv:2610.00324v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: $GW$+DMFT-type schemes replace the local part of a $GW$ self-energy by a separately computed local self-energy. A causal double counting removes a non-causal term from the hybridization (Lee and Haule, 2017), but the resulting total self-energy has been flagged as not guaranteed to be causal (Zhu and Chan, 2021). From the Herglotz representation, the spliced self-energy is causal if and only if its spectral measure is positive semi-definite. For translation-invariant single-band systems this becomes a momentum-resolved bound: the local weight may fall short of the local $GW$ weight by at most the momentum minimum of the $GW$ weight. On finite clusters, a mismatch between $GW$ and exact poles generically produces indefinite residues. On the Matsubara axis, a negative damping eigenvalue at one frequency certifies non-causality; passing does not establish causality. We examine these diagnostics in an idealized setting, not self-consistent $GW$+DMFT: one-shot $GW$ on the exact Green's function of small Hubbard clusters with the exact local self-energy inserted. At all 528 parameter sets, our computed $GW$ and exact self-energies pass both tests, as expected. The splice fails the pointwise test at 54 points, none at half filling, all at the lowest Matsubara frequency, and already at $U/t=0.5$; there the local $GW$ damping is 1.3-9 times the exact one. A block Pick test on eight frequencies, run with a second imaginary-time code, flags 481 of the 528 sets; for the other 47 it is inconclusive. Moment checks miss all of these, because the spliced high-frequency moment is exact. The Dyson Green's function is then non-causal too, yet passes the pointwise test everywhere tested. This version replaces a withdrawn one whose reported causality violations of $GW$ itself came from a sign error in the polarization; with the sign corrected, the computed $GW$ shows the expected positivity.

item.title: Hierarchical Response Theory of Electronegativity from Atomic Mean Inner Potential
item.description: arXiv:2610.29765v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Electronegativity remains conceptually ambiguous: is it a fixed atomic constant, or does it depend on the chemical environment? We resolve this debate by recasting electronegativity as a continuous response function rooted in the Atomic Mean Inner Potential (AMIP). Building on the established static scale \(\chi_{\mathrm{AMIP},1/2}\), we expand the electronegativity in fractional positive charge \(\delta\). The first-order term defines the Electrostatic Rigidity \(\mathcal{R}\), whose sign indicates whether an atom hardens or softens upon oxidation, and the second-order term defines the Electrostatic Anharmonic Modulus \(\mathcal{A}\). A logarithmic-derivative decomposition separates \(\mathcal{R}\) into an intrinsic, scale-independent response asymmetry \(\mathcal{D} \equiv \mathcal{R}_\Omega/\Omega_0 - \mathcal{R}_f/f_0\), which governs the competition between electronic screening loss (softening) and geometric volume collapse (hardening). Applying this to all 102 elements reveals a systematic dichotomy between softening main-group elements and hardening d-block elements, two scaling laws within the transition series, and two anomalies at half-filled d\(^5\) configurations and in Ce. The framework resolves the Cs--Fr controversy through relativistic analysis, reproduces classical electronegativity scales and Lewis acidity trends, and provides three falsifiable experimental predictions. It transforms electronegativity into a predictive, hierarchically structured quantum descriptor.
